title: Make your message clear
intro: I can choose words for what I need to communicate and check how the other person understands them.
exampleTitle: A question and a useful reply
example: Jo asks, “Where is the glue?” Kai replies, “Beside the blue paper,” and points to that paper where both can see it. The question needs a place, and the reply supplies one. The gesture helps identify the place. If Jo cannot see the pointing, Kai needs clearer words instead.
steps: 1. Ask and give the needed information
Start with what you want to find out. A useful reply answers that question. A closed question can invite yes or no; an open question invites more information.
Questions: “Is the bag here?” / “What did you put in the bag?” Reply to the second: “I packed a hat and a book.”
Which question invites a longer description? Why does the reply fit it?
“What did you put in the bag?” invites details about its contents. The reply names the packed things. “Is the bag here?” can be answered yes or no.
2. Notice what the message does
An offer says what you are willing to do; a request asks for an action. A command directs action, and an exclamation expresses a strong reaction. Similar words can have different jobs.
Messages: “I can carry that.” / “Could you carry that?” / “Put it on the bench.” / “What a huge box!”
Match each message to its job.
In order: offer, request, command and exclamation. A request can be phrased as a question. A calm command can end with a full stop; loudness alone does not decide the purpose.
3. Check words and other clues together
Words, facial expressions, signing and gestures can work together. A clue does not prove a hidden feeling. Ask when a reference or message is unclear.
Adult: put a pencil beside a book where both partners can see it. Say “Put it there” while pointing somewhere unclear, then invite clarification.
What could the listener ask before moving anything?
For example, “Do you mean this pencil, beside that book?” Name the object and place and check the response. Demonstrate the actual gesture; print alone does not show how it was received.
mistakes: “An offer and a request are the same.”
Ask who is offering help and who is asking for action.
“A face proves how someone feels.”
Use it as a clue and check the situation or ask.
“Everyone understands the same gesture.”
Meanings and communication preferences can vary; check understanding.
activity: Place a safe classroom object between two partners. Ask where it is, give a place answer, offer help with it and request an action. Finish with a calm instruction. Take turns and check that the replies fit.
adjust: Starter: model one short exchange with two purpose choices. Core: choose and respond to different message purposes. Stretch: keep the purpose when the listener cannot see your pointing, then explain the words you added.
safety: An adult can read and scribe; accept speech, signing or AAC. Do not require eye contact, smiling or touch. Observe the real exchange separately from a written answer. Cultural signs require a named community-endorsed source and local guidance.
tricky: 1. Is “Can I help you?” a request for the other person to carry your things?
It offers your help. Work out what the speaker is willing to do in this situation.
2. Can “Stand behind the line.” be a command when said calmly?
Yes. It directs an action; anger is not required.
3. If someone cannot see your point, is “there” always enough?
No. Name the place clearly or use a communication method the listener can access.
faq: Can we discuss a short film?

Yes. An adult supplies a suitable actual scene, pauses it and asks what the character said, what other clues were visible and what remains uncertain. Do not claim a film was watched from its description.
How should cultural communication be explored?
Use an actual named community-endorsed account and its local explanation. Ask what the account teaches about that specific context; do not invent or generalise a cultural sign.

title: Explain what you prefer and why
intro: I can name a like, dislike or preference and give a reason that explains it.
exampleTitle: A choice with a connected reason
example: Nia says, “I prefer building because I enjoy making tall towers.” Building is the choice; enjoying towers explains it. Eli can prefer drawing for a different reason. Neither person has to change a genuine preference to match the other.
steps: 1. Name the choice
Say what you like or dislike, or which option you prefer. A preference belongs to the person expressing it. Another person may choose differently.
Options: drawing a picture / building a model.
Which do you prefer, or would you choose something else?
Accept a genuine named choice, neither option or another activity. There is no single correct personal favourite. Ask the child to make the choice clear.
2. Connect a relevant reason
Because can connect a choice with its explanation. Check whether the reason says something useful about that choice, rather than merely repeating it.
“I like this story because the ending makes me laugh.” / “I like this story because I like it.”
Which gives more information about the choice?
The funny ending gives a specific reason. “Because I like it” repeats the preference. Ask neutrally what the person likes about it; do not supply their taste for them.
3. Compare for a stated purpose
A comparison can explain a choice. Better needs a purpose: better for which job? A practical comparison does not prove everyone has the same favourite.
Tray A holds six crayons. Pot B holds two. The job is carrying all six crayons in one container.
Which is better for this job? Give a reason with because.
Tray A is better for this job because it holds all six crayons. Someone could prefer Pot B for carrying just one or two. Use the supplied capacity facts, not an unseen size guess.
mistakes: “My favourite must be everyone’s favourite.”
Different connected reasons can support different choices.
“Because I like it explains the feature.”
Ask what about the choice the person likes.
“Better means best for every job.”
State the job and compare the relevant feature.
activity: Choose between two familiar activities. Tell a partner your preference and one connected reason. Listen to their choice, repeat what you heard and give your own view respectfully.
adjust: Starter: a choice and the frame “I prefer ___ because ___”. Core: a clear choice and relevant reason. Stretch: explain why two people can reasonably choose differently or why a different job changes the practical choice.
safety: Accept personal tastes without marking them wrong. Supply actual experiences when a reason depends on sound, taste or comfort; a picture cannot establish those sensations.
tricky: 1. Does because automatically make a reason relevant?
No. “I like the puzzle because the bus is late” does not explain this puzzle preference without another connection.
2. Can someone dislike a food you enjoy?
Yes. Listen to their reason and share yours without requiring agreement.
3. Must a comparison word end in -er?
No. Better compares too. Explain the feature or purpose rather than using a spelling rule.
faq: Can the reason be spoken?
Yes. An adult can scribe the learner’s own words. Check the explanation separately from spelling.
What if a reason is unclear?
Ask an open, neutral question such as “What do you like about it?” Then let the learner add a relevant detail.

title: Notice how a text’s job shapes its order
intro: I can compare short texts and explain how their order or grouping helps the reader.
example: Recount: “Yesterday we visited the garden. First we watered the beds. Then we picked beans.” Report: “Tools: a trowel and watering can. Jobs: watering and weeding.” The recount follows an event in time. The report groups information under headings. The topic is the same, but the organisation serves different purposes.
steps: 1. Follow connected events
A recount retells events, often using time order. A narrative tells a story with connected characters and events. Look at the whole text rather than deciding from one time word.
“A puppy found an empty bowl. It carried the bowl to Jo. Jo filled it with water.”
Why does the last event make sense after the first two?

The empty bowl and the puppy carrying it help us understand why Jo fills it. Moving the last event first would change how the story is revealed. Not every narrative needs the same problem-and-solution pattern.
2. Find information grouped for a job
Headings group related details so a reader can find information. A report is one kind of information text. Pictures, labels and diagrams may contribute to its organisation.
Garden report: Tools — trowel, watering can. Jobs — dig holes, water plants. New detail: sweep the path.
Where does the new detail belong, and why?
Under Jobs, because sweeping is an activity. The heading helps the reader find that kind of information without reading an event sequence.
3. Compare a view, an explanation and instructions
An opinion gives a view and may support it with a reason. An explanation tells how or why something happens. A procedure tells a reader what to do. Sequence alone does not decide the purpose.
Opinion: “I think we need shade because it helps us rest comfortably.” Explanation: “Water can freeze when it becomes cold enough.” Procedure: “Pour water into a tray. Put it in a freezer.”
Which directs actions, and which explains a change?
The procedure directs the actions. The explanation describes how water can change into ice. The opinion gives a view with a reason. Read the words and their organisation together.
mistakes: “Texts about the same topic have the same job.”
Compare what each text helps its reader do.
“A heading proves it is a report.”
Read the whole short text and how its information is grouped.
“Every sequence is a procedure.”
A recount or explanation can also use an order.
activity: Use a familiar class event. Tell a short recount with first and next, then state an opinion about the event with a reason. An adult scribes both texts. Compare what came first and what each text helps a listener understand.
adjust: Starter: sort two complete texts into their stated jobs. Core: explain the time order or grouping in a text. Stretch: keep a topic and change the text’s purpose, explaining the organisation you changed.
safety: Supply complete texts and read them aloud when decoding is not the target. Do not require knowledge of an unseen book or treat another curriculum’s year label as an Australian equivalence.
tricky: 1. Is a report the opposite of an information text?
No. A report is one way to organise information, often grouping facts about a topic.
2. Can a recount describe an imagined experience?
Yes. Real versus invented is not the only way to identify the organisation and purpose.
3. Do pictures only decorate a text’s structure?
No. Labels, diagrams or ordered images can help organise and communicate its information.
faq: Does every narrative need a problem?
No. Teach the connected events in the supplied story rather than impose one universal template.
What should an adult ask?
Ask “What is this text helping its reader do?” and “How does its order or grouping help?” Look for evidence in the complete text.

title: Hear how patterns connect a poem or chant
intro: I can notice repeated words, rhyming endings and spoken rhythm, then explain how they link the lines.
exampleTitle: A returning start and a matching ending
example: Say these original lines: “Tap, tap, by the tree. / Tap, tap, come with me.” Tap, tap returns at the start; tree and me rhyme at the ends. The pattern helps a listener anticipate the next line and join in. It also keeps the two lines sounding connected.
steps: 1. Notice what returns
Listen for repeated words, phrases or lines. Name exactly what returns and what changes. A repeated sentence frame can connect lines even without rhyme.
“Here comes rain. / Here comes wind. / Here comes sunshine.”
What repeats? Create another meaningful line using that start.
Here comes repeats; the final word changes. “Here comes night” is one possible new line. The returning frame makes the lines feel related.
2. Hear a rhyme in the whole line
Rhyming endings match in sound, not necessarily in spelling. Read or hear the complete lines and check that a new ending keeps a sensible meaning.
“A small frog sat upon a log. / Beside it slept a tired ___.” Choices: dog / hen.
Which ending keeps the rhyme and makes sense?
Dog rhymes with log and can be described as tired. Hen does not share that ending. Accept locally valid spoken rhymes when creating a fresh line.
3. Keep a beat while the word rhythm varies
A beat is a steady pulse. Rhythm is the timing of the spoken sounds. An adult can model two shorter syllables within one steady beat, so words do not all need one beat each.
Adult: make four evenly spaced taps. Say “tap | tap | lit-tle | tap”, fitting lit-tle inside the third tap. Model slowly, then invite an echo.
What stays steady, and which beat contains two spoken parts?
The four taps stay steady; little has two syllables within the third beat. Observe the actual echo. A written choice cannot demonstrate timing.
mistakes: “A poem is wrong unless it rhymes.”
Repetition or rhythm can connect lines without rhyme.
“Rhyming words need matching first letters.”
Compare their spoken endings.
“Every word gets one beat.”
Hear the model: two parts of little can fit inside one beat.
activity: An adult reads “Look, look, at the light. / Look, look, it is bright.” Identify Look, look and light/bright. Make another two-line pattern, then perform it at a manageable pace.
adjust: Starter: echo a repeated start. Core: identify repetition and rhyme and show the supplied rhythm. Stretch: create two connected lines and explain how returning words or matching sounds help a listener predict.
safety: Adults supply actual speech or singing; no recording is included here. Accept accessible tapping, pointing or movement and judge the sound pattern separately from motor speed or spelling.
tricky: 1. Can repetition link lines without rhyme?
Yes. Returning words or sentence frames can make them connected and predictable.
2. Are beat and syllable count always the same?
No. The timing of spoken syllables can vary against a steady beat.
3. If I choose a rhyming word that makes no sense, is the line finished?
Check both the sound and meaning. Revise the line so the pattern supports what you want to say.
faq: What does cohesion mean here?
The parts hold together: returning words and sound patterns help listeners connect the lines. The child can explain this in ordinary language.
Can we compare a poem, chant and song?
Yes. Supply and perform the actual texts. A chant uses spoken patterns; a song has a tune. Compare the patterns heard rather than rely only on the labels.

title: Find your way through books and screens
intro: I can use text features to locate information and explain the route I chose.
example: Model book: title “Our school garden”. Contents: Tools — page 2; Watering — page 4; Growing — page 6. To find watering information, read its contents entry, turn to page 4 and check the heading. A contents entry tells where a section starts; it does not contain all its information.
steps: 1. Use titles, headings and page numbers
The title names the whole text. A heading names a section. Contents entries and page numbers work together to guide you to that section.
Title: Our school garden. Contents: Tools 2; Watering 4; Growing 6.
Where does Growing start, and what should you check on arrival?
Page 6. Check its page number and Growing heading. Do not stop after reading the contents entry if you need the actual section information.
2. Follow the stated screen controls
Read a button or link’s label and the rules of that particular screen. Menus, scrolling and swipe directions can work differently across texts.
Model screen rules: Menu opens a list containing Tools, Watering and Growing. Selecting a section opens it. Next opens the next page; swiping left does the same on this model.
How would you open Watering from the section list?
Open Menu, then choose Watering. Next or a swipe might move one page, but the named section link is the supplied direct route. These rules belong to this model.
3. Compare routes and available actions

A print and screen feature may do a similar job through different actions. Images and labels help readers identify information. A verbal command works only when the device supports it and it is enabled.
Model screen: Watering tips is a link; Read aloud plays the text; Back returns to the previous screen. Enabled voice control also accepts “Go back”.
Which feature lets you hear the text? Give two stated ways to return.
Read aloud lets you hear it. Back or the enabled “Go back” command returns to the previous screen. These printed rules explain a model; actual device use must be observed separately.
mistakes: “Contents gives all the topic information.”
It directs you to a section.
“Every screen uses the same swipe direction.”
Read and learn that screen’s stated rules.
“Every device obeys a spoken command.”
Check support and whether voice control is enabled.
activity: An adult supplies a real information book and a safe familiar digital text. Choose one section to find using their actual headings, contents or controls. Explain the route and compare the actions used.
adjust: Starter: one target and two labelled choices. Core: follow a contents entry or named menu link and check the section. Stretch: compare two valid routes to the same information and explain which fits the task.
safety: An adult can read labels and supervise actual device use without choosing the route. A paper button or written route answer does not show that the learner has navigated a device.
tricky: 1. Can a digital book also have page numbers and contents?
Yes. Print and screen features can overlap. Compare their actual jobs.
2. Is an image always decoration?
No. A labelled picture can connect an object’s appearance with its name, as the retained watering-can example shows.
3. Should you press Next repeatedly if a direct section link is available?
Either may work under the model rules, but a named section link can be a more direct route. Check the destination.
faq: Must children use a particular brand of device?
No. Use available supervised resources and teach their actual controls.
What does successful navigation show?
The learner reaches the requested information and can explain which feature helped. Note any labels read or steps supplied by an adult.

title: Build one complete sentence idea
intro: I can recognise a complete idea, find its parts and add useful details.
exampleTitle: A longer sentence can still be simple
example: “The little bird sang softly in the tree.” names what is involved and tells a happening with useful details. It is one independent clause: a complete idea that can stand alone. “In the tree” alone only gives a place in this context. Length is not the test of a simple sentence.
steps: 1. Check the complete idea
Read the whole statement. Does it make sense by itself, or are you waiting for what happens or what is said about the named thing? Questions and commands can be complete too.
“The heavy bag” / “The bag is heavy.”
Which is a complete statement, and what does it tell?
The bag is heavy tells a state. The heavy bag only names something in this context. A sentence need not describe visible movement.
2. Keep the whole parts together
Ask who or what is involved and what is being said about it. A naming part can contain several words. Useful details can answer where, when or how.
“Our small class planted seeds in the garden.”
Which whole group names who planted? What happened, and where?
Our small class names who; planted seeds tells what happened; in the garden tells where. Seeds names something else involved. Do not reduce every meaningful group to one word.
3. Repair and expand without losing the idea
Say the intended whole idea before writing it. Supply a missing part or arrange the words sensibly. Add details without introducing another independent clause.
Words: the / puppy / rested. Then add a where detail.
Build a complete statement and add a sensible place.
The puppy rested. For example, The puppy rested beside the chair. The place detail keeps the one main idea. Capitals and end marks show a written boundary but cannot create missing meaning.
mistakes: “Short means complete.”
Check whether the idea stands alone.
“A verb must show movement.”
A state such as is heavy also completes an idea.
“Simple means exactly one verb word.”
The teacher criterion is one independent clause; length or a surface word count is not enough.
activityTitle: Say it, build it, expand it
activity: An adult says “The cat slept.” The learner makes a different complete statement, adds one where or when detail and reads it back. Compare it with a place phrase such as “under the bench”.
adjust: Starter: supplied who/what and happening cards. Core: create a complete statement and add one relevant detail. Stretch: explain why a longer version still has one independent clause and compare a complete calm command.
safety: Read and scribe when grammar is the target. Observe the learner’s own sentence production separately from choosing a supplied complete sentence. Formal clause diagrams are not required.
tricky: 1. Is “Close the gate.” complete even without a printed you?
Yes. In this command the person being addressed is understood.
2. Does a full stop make “Under the bench.” a complete statement?
In this standalone statement task it is still only a place phrase. Punctuation does not supply who or what and a happening or state.
3. Can “The bird is small.” be a simple sentence?
Yes. It is one complete clause describing a state rather than an action.
faq: Should we count words to find a simple sentence?
No. Check its complete clause and meaning. A sentence can include several useful details.
How can an adult help without giving the whole answer?
Ask who or what and what happens or is, then let the child supply and arrange the parts. Record any provided words.

title: Explore the jobs words do in a sentence
intro: I can explain naming words, verbs, qualities and details using the whole sentence.
example: “The small bird sang softly outside.” Bird names the animal, sang tells the happening, small describes the bird, softly tells how and outside tells where. Read the whole sentence before naming a word’s job. A word can do a different job in a different sentence.
steps: 1. Name participants and keep pronouns clear
Nouns name people, places, animals and things. Pronouns can refer to a noun or group. Make the reference clear; do not guess a person’s pronouns from a name or picture.
“The books fell. They landed on the mat.” / “Jo and I are ready.”
What does They refer to? Replace Jo and I with one pronoun.
They refers to the books. We can replace Jo and I because it includes the speaker and another person. The sentence supplies the reference.
2. Find doing, thinking and being verbs
A verb can tell a happening or state, including saying, thinking and being. It is not always an action you can see in a picture.
“The puppy runs.” / “The puppy is tired.” / “The child thinks.”
Find the verb in each sentence.
Runs, is and thinks are the verbs. Tired describes the puppy’s state; it is not the being verb in that sentence.
3. Add useful qualities and details
Adjectives describe qualities of nouns. Adverbs can add when, where or how; some details use groups of words instead. A more exact verb can also improve a sentence.
“The ducks swim slowly outside today.” / “The small ducks paddle beside the reeds.”
Which words tell how, where and when in the first sentence? What does small describe?

Slowly tells how, outside where and today when. Small describes the ducks. Beside the reeds is a group giving a place detail, not one adverb word. Paddle makes the movement more specific than swim in this context.
mistakes: “A word’s position always tells its job.”
Read its meaning in that particular sentence.
“All adverbs end in -ly.”
Today and outside can add details too.
“Every detail group is one adverb.”
Keep single words and groups distinct.
activity: Begin with “The child moved.” Choose a more exact verb such as tiptoed and a relevant detail. Explain what the change tells a reader. Then compare “We water the garden” with “The water is cold”.
adjust: Starter: find one named word job in a supplied sentence. Core: identify naming, verb, quality and detail meanings in context. Stretch: explain how water changes its job across the two sentences and create a clearer sentence.
safety: An adult can read or scribe. Use actual or supplied facts for descriptions; a monochrome picture cannot establish colour, weight or texture. Accept clear pronoun references without guessing gender.
tricky: 1. Is water always a noun?
No. It is a verb in “We water the garden” and a noun in “The water is cold”.
2. Is softly a quality of the bird in “The bird sang softly”?
It tells how the bird sang. Small in “The small bird” describes the bird.
3. Can a thinking word be a verb?
Yes. Thinks and hopes can tell processes without visible movement.
faq: Do we need advanced word-class labels?
Use the familiar noun, pronoun, verb, adjective and adverb labels with meaningful examples. Avoid sorting isolated ambiguous words by guesswork.
What makes a sentence improvement useful?
It adds accurate meaning: a precise verb, quality or relevant when, where or how detail. More words alone do not guarantee clarity.

title: Compare what images add to a text
intro: I can point to visible image clues and explain how they help a story, diagram or sequence.
example: Both supplied pictures show a duck. The careful drawing shows its shape; the cartoon adds a scarf and smile to create a playful character. The difference is useful for comparing an information picture with a story illustration. Neither style is automatically best for every purpose.
steps: 1. Compare visible details and purpose
Start with what is actually shown, then explain how it helps the text. A drawing is not a photograph. A cartoon’s added features can help create a character.
Use the duck comparison directly below: a careful drawing beside a scarf-wearing cartoon.
Which suits a playful duck story? Give one visible reason.
The cartoon’s scarf and smile help create a playful character. The careful drawing can help show a real duck’s shape. Explain the purpose and clue rather than choose a favourite style.
2. Read words and pictures together
Words and images can share meaning or contribute different details. A mismatch may be important, so check both rather than ignore one.
Story words: “The room was empty.” The supplied picture shows a kitten under a chair.
What does the image add or make you question?
An animal is still in the room. The reader should notice the mismatch with empty and consider what the words mean in the story. The image alone does not provide the kitten’s name or the time.
3. Use labels and ordered stages
A label line connects a name with a visible part. A sequence shows selected stages in order. Compare the job of each image.
Use the supplied labelled flower and First–Next–Last plant sequence directly below.
Which image identifies the leaf? Which shows a change over stages?
The labelled flower links leaf to that part. The sequence shows the seed becoming a small plant and then a taller flowering plant. It does not give an exact number of days.
mistakes: “The picture proves every hidden feeling.”
Point to the clue and keep uncertain interpretations tentative.
“A larger drawing proves a larger real object.”
Printed size may be a design choice; look for actual size information.
“Every image serves the same job.”
Compare character, location, named-part, sequence or invitation meanings.
activity: Use the supplied retained duck story, information picture and story-time poster. Read their headings and point to a detail supporting each job. With an adult, create a simple diagram of a familiar object with two accurate labels.
adjust: Starter: choose between two stated image jobs with the pictures visible. Core: compare two images and cite visible details. Stretch: explain one meaning supplied by words and a different meaning supplied by an image, including a supported mismatch.
safety: All comparison images are supplied in their teaching sections. Cultural-account work needs the actual attributed source and its guidance; do not infer a cultural symbol’s meaning or imitate the artwork. An adult may read captions.
tricky: 1. Does a picture show everything outside its frame?
No. Explain what is visible and keep claims about unseen people, objects or events uncertain.
2. Is the careful duck drawing a photograph?
No. It is a drawing. Compare its useful detail with the cartoon without changing its medium label.
3. Does the plant sequence tell exactly how long growth took?
No. It shows selected stages. Exact elapsed time would need additional information.
faq: Can we explore a First Nations Australian artwork?

An adult can supply the National Museum of Australia’s actual Holiday Time by Eunice Yunurupa Porter and its Year 1 digital flip book and teacher guidance. Follow cultural notices, use the artist’s account and distinguish visible detail from meanings you have not been taught.
What makes an answer strong?
It names a visible clue, connects it with the text’s job and avoids unsupported details. Different interpretations may be valid when the evidence supports them.

title: Use words that fit the learning topic
intro: I can explain a taught topic word, use it accurately and check its meaning in context.
exampleTitle: A meaning, not just a repeated word
example: In a plant lesson, root, stem and leaf name parts. Observe means look closely to find out. “I observe the leaf” uses both words meaningfully. Repeating observe without showing what it means is different from understanding it. Use a real safe plant or the supplied retained plant image to connect words with their meanings.
steps: 1. Group by a stated topic
Topic words help us discuss what we are learning. Group them by meaning in this context rather than their first letters. A word may be useful in more than one subject.
Topic: weather. Words: rain, wind, pencil, cloud.
Which word does not name weather in this set? Explain.
Pencil names a writing tool; the others name weather features. The topic is stated so the grouping has a clear purpose.
2. Use the context to choose a meaning
A definition, action, picture or surrounding sentence can explain a new word. Try the meaning in that context and check it with an adult.
“A seedling is a young plant. We looked closely at the seedling.” / “Measure the ribbon’s length: how long it is.”
What do seedling and length mean here?
Seedling means a young plant. Length means how long the ribbon is, not its weight or colour. The supplied explanations make this a meaning task rather than untaught science or maths recall.
3. Choose precisely and compare contexts
Related words can do different jobs. The same spelling can also have different meanings across situations. Read the whole message before choosing.
A route is a way from one place to another; a map key explains symbols. “Turn the page.” / “It is my turn.”
Which word names a way to go? Does turn have the same meaning in both sentences?
Route names a way to go. In the first sentence turn means an action on the page; in the second it means a person’s time to take part. The surrounding words decide.
mistakes: “Words with the same first letter belong together.”
Use the stated topic and word meanings.
“Every season has the same weather everywhere.”
Use the actual place and context; avoid universal weather claims.
“Knowing a word means only saying it back.”
Explain, show or use the meaning.
activity: Choose one taught classroom topic word. Explain it, show it with a safe object, image or action, and use it in a short sentence. Your partner explains it back. Revisit an unclear meaning with a different example.
adjust: Starter: two taught words and a supplied meaning or object. Core: explain and use a topic word accurately. Stretch: compare a word in two complete contexts and explain what changes or stays the same.
safety: Read directions and supply all required definitions. Check vocabulary separately from spelling and handwriting. Local Country names, pronunciation and protocols must be verified through local community guidance.
tricky: 1. Does a word belong to only one school subject?
No. Measure or pattern can be useful across subjects; explain the meaning in the particular task.
2. Does Country only mean a location on a map?

In First Nations Australian contexts it includes enduring cultural connections, responsibilities and relationships with place. Follow the particular community’s guidance rather than reduce it to a generic map label.
3. Are a Welcome to Country and an Acknowledgement the same?

No. An Acknowledgement can show anyone’s respect for Traditional Owners and continuing connection to Country. A Welcome is delivered by Traditional Owners or authorised First Nations people. Use adult-verified local protocols.
faq: Which words support respectful school acknowledgements?

An adult can teach Country, Traditional Owners and Acknowledgement of Country using Reconciliation Australia and local community guidance. Learn what the terms mean and why they are used; do not invent local names or a universal ceremonial script.
How do we avoid testing untaught facts?
Provide a clear meaning, object or context before asking the learner to use a new topic word. The goal here is vocabulary understanding.

title: Use capitals and end marks for a clear message
intro: I can choose punctuation for the message, capitalise familiar names and check my writing.
exampleTitle: Read the two messages before editing
example: “mia has a kite where is ben” contains a telling idea and a direct question. Write: “Mia has a kite. Where is Ben?” Mia and Ben are names, each sentence starts with a capital, and the question ends with ?. Read the two sentences aloud and notice their boundaries; a pause alone does not always require a full stop.
steps: 1. Match the end mark to the message
A full stop can end a calm statement or instruction. A question mark ends a direct question. An exclamation mark can show strong feeling, surprise or urgency when the context supports it.
A calm statement: “The gate is shut”. A direct question: “Is the gate shut”. An excited reaction: “What a wonderful surprise”.
Choose a fitting end mark for each supplied context.
The gate is shut. Is the gate shut? What a wonderful surprise! Purpose and context guide the marks; not every instruction needs an exclamation mark.
2. Capitalise particular names
Use capitals for familiar proper nouns such as a person, pet, place or holiday name, wherever the name appears. Ordinary words do not all need capitals.
“sam visits canberra on australia day.” The supplied names are Sam, Canberra and Australia Day.
Write the sentence with the supplied names capitalised.
Sam visits Canberra on Australia Day. Sam also starts the sentence. The common words visits and on stay lower case; Australia Day is the supplied two-word holiday name.
3. Edit, write and read back
Check complete ideas and boundaries, then sentence starts, I, names and end marks. Read the result aloud to see whether it communicates the intended meaning.
“i have a book can i read it” is a calm statement followed by a question.
Edit it, then create a different statement and question of your own.

I have a book. Can I read it? For the fresh pair, accept complete meaningful sentences with a suitable full stop and question mark, correct starts, I and any names. Note support; choosing a correction is not the same as writing independently.
mistakes: “Every spoken pause needs a full stop.”
Check whole sentence boundaries and meaning.
“Every command needs !.”
A calm “Wait here.” can use a full stop; urgency may support “Wait here!”.
“Only names at the start need capitals.”
Particular names need capitals inside sentences too.
activityTitle: A tiny note with two purposes
activity: Write or dictate a calm statement and direct question about a familiar object. Include one familiar supplied name. Check capitals and endings, then read both to a partner, noticing the boundaries and intended expression.
adjust: Starter: choose . or ? for supplied clear contexts. Core: write or dictate a statement and a question with capitals. Stretch: compare Wait here. with Wait here! and explain contexts that suit each, then edit a fresh two-sentence note.
safety: An adult can provide the exact spelling of names. Check punctuation and capitals separately from handwriting. Listen to actual reading when assessing pauses and expression; print does not demonstrate oral performance.
tricky: 1. Is “I asked for a pencil.” a direct question?
No. It reports asking, so a full stop can fit this calm statement.
2. Must ordinary season words have capitals inside a sentence?
No. Names of days, months and holidays take capitals; an ordinary word such as summer usually stays lower case.
3. Can the same words use . or ! in different contexts?
Yes. “Wait here.” can be calm, while “Wait here!” can be urgent. Supply the context before demanding one answer.
faq: Does a rising voice always prove a question?
No. Use the words and intended message as well as actual reading. Voice patterns can vary.
What should an adult check in a written answer?
Check the complete ideas, suitable boundaries and end marks, sentence starts, I and familiar names. Record any dictated or supplied support.
